turns.text: Hi Doug, it's Priya from the upstairs unit on Maple Street. Sorry to call so early, but the furnace stopped working sometime last night. When I woke up, the thermostat said fourteen degrees, and it's minus twenty outside.
Oh no, that's not good at all. Is the thermostat screen still on, or is it completely blank?
The screen is on. It says the heat is on, and I can hear a click, but no warm air comes out of the vents. I checked the breaker panel like you showed me in the fall, and nothing has tripped.
Okay, good thinking. Then it's probably the igniter again. The exact same thing happened two winters ago with the previous tenants.

Here's the thing. My usual technician, Marco, is booked solid until Thursday afternoon. I could call one of those twenty-four-hour emergency companies, but they charge almost triple, and honestly, the quality is hit or miss.
Thursday is three days away, though. I work from home, so I'd be sitting here in my winter coat all day.

No, you're right, that's not fair to you. How about this? I'll drop off two electric space heaters on my way to work this morning, and I'll call the emergency company anyway. If they can come today, great. If they can't come before tomorrow evening, we'll just wait for Marco.
That sounds reasonable. Just so you know, the bedroom and the office share one circuit, so I can't run both heaters back there at the same time.
Good point. Put one in the living room and one in the bedroom, then.
Okay, quick update. The emergency company can send someone between two and five this afternoon. Will you be home?
I have a dentist appointment at three thirty, unfortunately. It took me two months to get it, so I'd really rather not move it.

Don't cancel it. I'll leave work early and let the technician in myself. I still have the spare key. And Priya, I'll take fifty dollars off this month's rent to cover the extra hydro from those heaters.
That's really kind of you. Thanks, Doug. I'll leave the side gate unlocked so they can get to the basement door without any trouble.
Morning, Amira. You look like you've had a rough start to the day.

Oh, hi Kevin. I've been up since half past six trying to register Yusuf for swimming lessons at the community centre. Registration opened online at seven, and by ten past, every Saturday class for his level was full.
Ah, the famous seven a.m. rush. The same thing happened to us last spring. Did you put his name on the waitlist?
I did, but he's number twenty-three. I can't see him getting in this session.

Probably not. But here's something most people don't know. The city also runs lessons at the pool in the high school on Elm Road. They're on weeknights, so they don't fill up nearly as fast. My daughter Chloe goes there on Tuesdays and Thursdays at six.
Weeknights could be tricky. I don't get home from my shift at the hospital until quarter to six most days.
Well, I drive Chloe anyway. If Yusuf ended up in the same time slot, I could take them both, and you could pick them up at seven when the class finishes.
Kevin, that would be amazing. Are you sure it's not too much trouble?
Not at all. Honestly, Chloe would love having a friend there. She keeps complaining that she doesn't know anyone in her group.
Then I'll check the website tonight. If there's a spot, I'll grab it before somebody else does.
Do it soon. Those classes don't fill up in ten minutes, but they do fill up.
Hi, I'd like to get a library card, please. My family and I just moved here last month.
Welcome! Cards are free for anyone who lives in the city. I'll just need one piece of photo ID and something that shows your address here, like a lease or a utility bill.
I have my passport and our lease agreement. Is that enough?

Perfect. Your card lets you borrow up to fifty items at a time. Books are three weeks, and DVDs and video games are one week. There are no late fines on children's materials anymore, but adult items are twenty-five cents a day.
My wife is mostly interested in improving her English. Do you have anything for that?

Lots. We have free conversation circles every Wednesday evening at seven, right here in the community room. You don't need to register, just drop in. They're run by volunteers, and the groups are small, so everyone gets a chance to talk. We also have an online language program that she can use at home with her card number.
That's great. And my son is eight. He reads all the time.

Then he should have his own card. Children under twelve need a parent to sign for them, so you can do that today while you're here. In the summer, we also run a reading challenge where kids collect a stamp for every book they finish.
He'll love that. One more question. I saw a sign by the door about museum passes?

Yes, that's one of our most popular services. You can borrow a free family pass for several local museums and the science centre. New passes are released online every Monday at nine, and they go very quickly, so set an alarm.
Thank you, this is very helpful.
My pleasure. Let me get your card started.

Drivers in the city will have to find somewhere else to park overnight this winter, after council voted last night to expand its seasonal parking ban. Starting December first, parking on residential streets will be banned between one a.m. and seven a.m. on any night when a snow event is declared. Until now, the ban applied only to main roads and bus routes. City staff say parked cars were the biggest reason plows could not properly clear side streets last winter, leaving narrow, icy lanes that slowed down ambulances and fire trucks. The vote was eight to three. Councillors who opposed the change said it will be hardest on people in older neighbourhoods, where many houses were built without driveways. Councillor Teresa Lam, who represents one of those areas, said residents are being asked to solve a problem without being given any real alternatives. In response, council agreed to open four municipal parking lots free of charge on snow event nights. Residents can sign up for text or email alerts on the city's website, and snow events will also be announced on local radio by eight p.m. the evening before. Vehicles left on the street during a ban can be ticketed ninety dollars and may be towed if they block a plow. However, the city says it will give out warnings instead of tickets for the first two weeks of December while people get used to the new rules. Officials expect about twenty snow events in an average winter.

Thanks for staying a few minutes. As you know, I've been asked to organize the holiday food drive again, and honestly, last year was disappointing. We filled maybe three boxes, and most of it was canned corn.
To be fair, it was announced the week before the holidays. Half the office was already on vacation.
That's true. So this year, I want to start in mid-November and run it for three weeks. The question is how we make it work better.

Can I suggest something? My sister volunteers at the food bank, and she says they actually prefer money. They can buy food in bulk for much less than we pay at the grocery store, and they can buy exactly what they're short on.
I get that, but people like giving something they can see. If it's just a link in an email, everyone will mean to do it and then forget.
Maybe we do both. Boxes in the lobby for people who want to bring food, and a donation link for people who'd rather give money.
And what about a competition between departments? Finance against marketing, that sort of thing. Nothing motivates accountants like a scoreboard.
I'd be careful there. Some people on my team are supporting family back home, and money's tight for them. If we post totals by department, they might feel pressured, or feel judged for not giving.
That's a fair point. What if we only tracked the office total? Like a big thermometer poster in the lobby that fills up as we get closer to our goal.
I can live with that. It's still visible, which is what I care about. And maybe the whole office gets something if we hit the target, like a pancake breakfast.
I like that much better. Everyone wins, and nobody's singled out.
Great. Ben, could you call the food bank and ask which items they're shortest on? I'd rather put a specific list on the boxes than end up with another mountain of corn.
Sure, I'll call them first thing tomorrow.
And I'll set up the donation page. My sister can tell me which option sends the money straight to them without any fees.
Perfect. I'll talk to management about the breakfast.

The city's plan to add a protected bike lane along Front Street has become one of the most heated debates in town this year, and after speaking with people on all sides, I can see why. The proposal would remove about sixty on-street parking spaces along a one-kilometre stretch and replace them with a cycling lane separated from traffic by a concrete curb. For many store owners on Front Street, those parking spaces are the heart of the issue. The owner of a hardware store that has been there for over forty years told me that most of his customers buy things they can't carry on a bike, like bags of soil, paint and lumber. Take away the parking, he said, and they'll simply drive to the big stores out by the highway. Several other owners share that fear, and a petition against the plan has collected more than a thousand signatures. Cycling groups see it very differently. They point out that Front Street is the most direct route between the university and downtown, and that it has had more collisions involving cyclists than any other street in the city over the past five years. In their view, the question isn't whether people will cycle on Front Street, because they already do. It's whether they'll do it safely. Interestingly, not every business owner is opposed. The manager of a cafe near the university told me most of her customers already arrive on foot or by bike. She also mentioned a city survey of shoppers in the area, which found that people who walk or cycle tend to visit more often, even if they spend a little less each time. She'd welcome the lane, but only if the city keeps some short-term parking and a loading zone for deliveries. That idea of a middle ground seems to be gaining support. Some councillors now suggest a one-year pilot using temporary barriers instead of concrete, along with a few fifteen-minute parking spots on each block. If the sales and safety numbers look good after a year, the lane could become permanent. If not, the barriers come out. For a debate that has divided the street for months, a trial run may be the most sensible way forward.
Tom, I just got off the phone with the truck rental place. Bad news. The small cube van we wanted is gone for Saturday. Everyone's moving at the end of the month.
Seriously? I thought we booked it last week.
We put it on hold, but we never paid the deposit, so they gave it to someone else. They still have a twenty-foot truck, but it's forty dollars more a day, and I've never driven anything that big.

I drove one when my brother moved to Calgary. It's not as scary as it sounds, as long as you take the corners wide. Let's take it. To be honest, our couch probably wouldn't have fit in the small one anyway.
What about the elevators? Did you call the new building?
Yes. The property manager said we have to book the freight elevator at least forty-eight hours ahead, and there's a two-hundred-dollar damage deposit. We get it back if nothing gets scratched.
Two hundred? Wow. And our building here only lets people move out between nine and noon on weekends, right?
Right. So if we start loading at nine sharp, we should be at the new place by about one. I asked for the elevator from one to five.
Perfect. I'll pick up some of those padded moving blankets to cover the walls of the elevator, just to be safe. I really want that deposit back.
Last thing. How many people do we have helping us carry everything? Because I am not lifting that bookshelf with just the two of us.
My cousin Raj said yes, and Leah from work can come too, but only after eleven, because her son has a swimming lesson in the morning.
That works. We can carry down the boxes and the small things first, and save the heavy furniture for when she gets here. I'll order pizza for everyone at the new place around two, as a thank-you.
Sounds good. I'll text everyone the new address tonight, plus the buzzer code, so nobody gets stuck outside.
Hey Danny, do you have a minute? I'm trying to finalize the plan for Thanksgiving dinner.
Sure. Are we still doing it at your place on the Sunday?
Yes, Sunday at five. Mom wanted Monday, but half of us have to drive home that day, so Sunday makes more sense. The thing is, I'm a bit worried about the menu this year.
Why? Your turkey is always great.

It's not the turkey. Dad's doctor told him to cut way down on salt, and you know Mom's stuffing is basically salt with a bit of bread in it. I don't want Dad to feel left out, but I also don't want to hurt Mom's feelings by asking her to change her recipe.
Honestly, I think Mom would rather know. Just tell her directly. She'd be a lot more upset if Dad ended up eating something he shouldn't.
You're probably right. I'll call her tonight. Now, about you and Lena. Lena's still vegetarian, right?
She is, but please don't make anything special. She said she'll bring a big squash and lentil dish that everyone can share. She made it for my birthday, and people loved it.
Perfect, that takes one thing off my list. And what time are you two leaving Montreal?
That's the other thing. I have to work until noon on Sunday, so we won't be on the road before one. With holiday traffic, we might not make it by five.
Don't stress. Just text me from the road, and we'll wait to carve the turkey until you get here. We'll have pie first, then.
Ha. Dad would love that.
Hi, I just moved here for school, and I'm trying to figure out the best way to pay for the bus.
Sure, happy to help. Most people use our reloadable fare card. The card itself costs six dollars, and then you load money or a pass onto it. You just tap it on the reader when you get on.
Is it cheaper than paying cash?

A little. A cash fare is three thirty-five, and with the card it's three ten. But the bigger benefit is transfers. When you tap, you automatically get ninety minutes to transfer to any other bus or the train at no extra charge. With cash, you have to ask the driver for a paper transfer, and a lot of people forget.
I'll be going to the college five days a week. Would a monthly pass make more sense?

Definitely. The regular monthly pass is one hundred and ten dollars, but full-time college and university students can get one for seventy-five. You don't buy that one here, though. You order it through your college's student services office, and they load it onto your card.
Oh, good to know. Is there anything else I should do with the card?
Register it online. It only takes a few minutes, and if you lose the card, we can cancel it and move your balance to a new one. If it isn't registered, that money is just gone.
Okay. One more thing. My mother is coming to visit for two weeks next month. She's sixty-eight. Can she get a seniors' discount?

The seniors' card is only for local residents, unfortunately, because you have to show proof of an address here. For a two-week visit, I'd suggest a seven-day pass for each week. It's thirty-two dollars and covers unlimited rides, so she can explore the city as much as she likes.
Perfect. Then I'll get a fare card for myself today.

A breakfast program that started at a single elementary school three years ago is now coming to every school in the district. The school board announced on Tuesday that all thirty-one of its elementary and middle schools will offer free breakfast to students starting in January. The program began at Riverside Elementary, where a group of parents noticed that some children were arriving at school hungry. They began serving toast, fruit and yogurt in the gym before the morning bell. Teachers there say the difference was clear. According to the school's principal, fewer students came to the office complaining of stomach aches, and classes settled down more quickly in the morning. The expansion will be paid for with a mix of provincial funding and donations from local businesses, including two grocery stores that have agreed to supply fresh fruit at cost. The board stresses that breakfast will be open to every student, not only those from families in need. Officials say this avoids singling anyone out, which was one reason some families stayed away from earlier programs. The board is now looking for about two hundred volunteers to help set up and serve food each morning from seven forty-five to eight fifteen. Volunteers will need a police background check, which the board will pay for. Parents who would like to help can contact their school office or attend an information night at the board office next Thursday.

Let's move on to the last item, the electric vehicle chargers. Six owners have now asked about installing them in the parking garage, so I asked an electrician for a quote. For ten chargers, including upgrading the electrical panel, it came to about forty-eight thousand dollars.
Forty-eight thousand? Marie, I don't even own a car anymore. Why should my condo fees pay for someone else's fuel?
Nobody's suggesting the building pay for their electricity, Gordon. Each charger would have its own meter, so drivers would pay for what they use.
Fine, but the installation would still come out of the reserve fund, and that money is supposed to be for things like the roof.
That's a real concern. The roof is due to be replaced in about four years, and we can't touch that money.

But think about resale. More and more buyers ask about charging before they even look at a unit. In five years, a building without it will be harder to sell, and that affects everyone's property value, including yours.
Maybe. I'm not planning to sell any time soon.

Here's something the electrician suggested. The expensive part is the panel upgrade and running the wiring through the garage. What if the building paid only for that, and any owner who wanted a charger bought and installed their own unit at their parking spot?
That makes sense. The wiring benefits the whole building, but the chargers themselves are personal.
How much would the building's part cost, then?
About twenty thousand. He also mentioned a rebate program that might cover up to half of that, though we'd have to apply, and it isn't guaranteed.
Ten thousand is a lot easier to swallow than forty-eight. But I still think every owner should have a say, not just the three of us.
Agreed. Let's send out a survey this month and bring the results to the annual general meeting in March.
I'll draft the survey. I'll keep it short, or nobody will fill it out.

Across the region, more employers are asking staff who have worked from home for the past few years to come back to the office for at least part of the week. One large insurance company downtown recently told its employees that, starting in the new year, they will be expected in the office three days a week. The reaction has been mixed, to say the least. The managers I spoke with mostly made the same argument: some things are simply harder to do through a screen. One department head told me her biggest worry is new hires. Experienced staff know who to ask and how things work, she said, but people who joined in the last few years have learned almost everything over video calls. Many of them have never had the chance to just overhear how a senior colleague handles a difficult client. Many employees, on the other hand, say the policy ignores how much their lives have changed. A claims adjuster who lives about an hour outside the city told me that going in three days a week means six extra hours of commuting, plus the cost of parking downtown. He also pointed out that his own work, which is mostly reviewing files and writing reports, gets done faster at home, where there are fewer interruptions. What surprised me was hearing from younger workers who actually want to go back, at least some of the time. A twenty-four-year-old analyst told me that working from her small apartment had become lonely, and that she felt she was missing chances to be noticed by people who could help her career. Downtown business owners, not surprisingly, are strongly in favour. Restaurants and dry cleaners near the office towers say their weekday sales have never fully recovered. So where does that leave us? It seems clear that a single rule for everyone will leave somebody unhappy. The employers that seem to be handling this best are the ones letting each team decide which days to come in, based on the work it actually does, rather than setting one policy from the top.
Lakeview Property Management, this is Gord speaking.

Hi Gord, it's Priya Sharma in unit 304 at the Birchwood building. I'm sorry to call so early, but the heat in my apartment stopped working sometime overnight. When I woke up, the thermostat said fourteen degrees, and it's minus twenty-five outside.
Oh no, that's not good. Is it just your unit, or have you heard from any of your neighbours?

I knocked on 302 on my way down to get the paper, and they said their place is fine. The radiators in my bedroom and living room are completely cold, though. I tried turning the thermostat up and down, and I even changed the batteries, but nothing happened.
Okay. So it sounds like it's something specific to your unit, rather than the boiler for the whole building.
Here's the thing. Our regular heating contractor is booked solid this morning because of the cold snap. The earliest they can get to you is tomorrow, between eight and noon. I know that's not ideal.
Tomorrow? I'm not sure I can sleep in here tonight. I have a ten-month-old baby, and it's only going to get colder.

Understood. I can offer you two things. First, I can drop off two electric space heaters within the hour. They'll keep a couple of rooms comfortable. Or, if you'd rather, the company keeps a furnished guest suite on the ground floor for situations like this. It's small, but the heat works, and you're welcome to stay there tonight at no charge.
The guest suite sounds better, honestly. I'd worry about leaving space heaters on all night with the baby crawling around.
That makes sense. I'll bring the key up to you myself.
One more thing. Will someone need to get into my unit tomorrow if I'm downstairs?
Yes, the technician will need to get at the radiators and the valve in your hall closet. If you'd like to be there, just let me know. Otherwise, I can let them in and stay with them the whole time.
I'd like to be there, actually. I want to ask them whether the radiator in the bedroom is the problem, because it's been making a clicking noise for a few weeks now.
Good to know. I'll put that in the work order. And for what it's worth, since you've been without heat, we'll take a day off this month's rent. You'll see it as a credit on your February statement.
That's really kind of you. Thanks, Gord.
Tomas, have you got a minute? I want to sort out the potluck for Mrs. Dubois before she moves to Kelowna.
Sure. Are we still doing it on Saturday the twelfth?

That was the plan, but the community room in our building is booked that day for a yoga class. The superintendent said it's free on Sunday the thirteenth, from four until nine. Does that work for you?
Sunday's actually better for me. I work until three on Saturdays anyway. How many people are coming?
I've heard back from fourteen neighbours so far, and a few more might show up. I was thinking we'd ask everyone to bring a dish, and the two of us will cover the drinks, the plates and a card.
Sounds good. I can pick up the card and get people to sign it in the lobby this week. What should I bring for food?
Well, Mrs. Dubois is always going on about your butter tarts. Would you mind making a batch?
Ha, I suppose I could. Although the last time I made them, half of them stuck to the pan. I'll use paper liners this time.
Perfect. Oh, and one more thing. Let's not tell her it's a farewell party. Her daughter is going to bring her down and say it's just a building meeting.
A surprise? She'll love that. Just make sure nobody mentions it in the elevator. You know how people talk in this building.
Good point. I'll put a note about it on the invitations.
Good afternoon, Riverside Public Library, Laura speaking. How can I help?
Hi there. I've just moved to the city with my family, and a friend told me the library has programs for newcomers. I was hoping you could tell me a bit about them.

Absolutely, and welcome! The first thing you'll want is a library card. It's free for anyone who lives in the city. You just need one piece of photo ID and something with your current address on it, like a lease or a utility bill. If you've only just moved and don't have a bill yet, a letter from your landlord is fine.
That's good to know, because we haven't had our first hydro bill yet, and the lease is still with the landlord. What about my kids? They're seven and eleven.

Children under fourteen can have their own cards, but a parent has to sign for them in person. And we stopped charging late fines on children's books two years ago, so you won't need to worry about that.
Great. My wife is keen to practise her English. Is there anything for that?

Yes, we run conversation circles twice a week, Tuesday evenings at seven and Thursday mornings at ten. They're drop-in, so there's no need to register, and they're led by trained volunteers. The Thursday group tends to be smaller, so people often find it easier to speak up there.
She'd probably like that one, then. She's a bit shy at first. And is there any help with job searching? I'm an accountant, but I'm told my credentials need to be assessed here.

We have a settlement worker from a local agency who's at our branch every Wednesday afternoon. She can explain how credential recognition works and help with your resume. You do need to book that one, though, because the slots fill up quickly. I can put your name down now if you like.
Yes, please. That would be wonderful.

Drivers and transit riders in the east end will need to plan ahead starting Monday, when the Harbour Street Bridge closes for six weeks of repairs. City engineers say the work is needed after an inspection last spring found cracks in several of the bridge's steel supports. The bridge is not considered dangerous at the moment, but officials say waiting another year would make the repairs far more expensive. During the closure, traffic will be detoured along Mill Road, which is expected to add about ten minutes to a typical rush-hour trip. To ease congestion, the city is adding a temporary bus route, the 47 Express, which will run every twelve minutes between the east-end park-and-ride lot and downtown. Rides on the new route will be free for the first two weeks. Cyclists and pedestrians will still be able to cross the bridge on a narrow lane on the north side, except on the two weekends when crews are paving. Those dates will be posted on the city's website. Not everyone is happy with the timing. Business owners on Harbour Street say the closure comes right in the middle of their busy summer season. The owner of one cafe told reporters she expects to lose about a third of her customers. A city spokesperson responded that summer is the only time of year when the concrete can be poured properly, and that the city will put up signs reminding residents that shops on the street remain open. The bridge is scheduled to reopen before the Labour Day long weekend.
Okay, so the good news is that the city approved our grant. We've got four thousand dollars, and it has to be spent by the end of March. I'd like us to agree on priorities today.

Well, for me the obvious one is the water. Half the plots are still watered by people hauling cans from the tap beside the shed. Our older members really struggle with that, and a couple of them told me they might give up their plots.

I don't disagree, but have you priced out an irrigation system? The quote I got last year was close to three thousand dollars, and that was before installation. It would eat up nearly the whole grant.
It doesn't have to be a full system. A few extra taps along the main path would make a huge difference, and that's much cheaper.
That's a fair compromise. Callum, what was your priority?

Raised beds. We have twelve people on the waiting list, and three of them use wheelchairs. Right now there's nowhere for them to garden. Four accessible raised beds would be maybe twelve hundred dollars in lumber and soil.
I like that, especially since our application talked about accessibility. The city will expect to see something along those lines in our final report.
Agreed. I'd just want to make sure we don't build them in the corner by the back fence. That's in shade most of the day.
Point taken. We could put them near the entrance, which would make them easier to reach, too.
So we're looking at extra taps and the raised beds. That still leaves some money. I was going to suggest a tool library, a shed of shared tools so people don't have to bring their own.
Honestly, we already have a shed full of tools that nobody puts back. I'd rather spend the rest on something educational, like a composting workshop.
Or we could hold some back. Something always breaks in the spring.
Let's not decide that today. I'll get quotes on the taps. Callum, could you sketch out the raised beds?
Sure, I'll have something ready by the next meeting.

Few sounds signal autumn in the suburbs quite like the roar of a gas-powered leaf blower. But in the town of Westbrook, that sound may soon disappear. Town council is considering a bylaw that would ban gas leaf blowers starting in 2028, and the proposal has divided residents. Supporters say the issue is about more than noise. The resident who started the petition, a nurse who works night shifts, says she is woken up almost every afternoon in October by blowers on her street. Others point to air quality. Small two-stroke engines burn fuel inefficiently, and supporters argue that running one for an hour can produce more pollution than a long drive in a car. Electric blowers, they say, have improved to the point where they can do the job for most homeowners. Landscaping companies see it differently. The owner of a local lawn care business says battery-powered equipment works fine on a small lawn, but his crews look after large properties all day. He estimates he would need three batteries for every machine, and recharging them between jobs isn't practical. He warns that customers would end up paying more for fall clean-ups. He says he isn't against change, but he wants a longer phase-in and some financial help for small businesses. A third group would like a compromise. Some councillors have suggested limiting the hours when gas blowers can be used, for example banning them before nine in the morning and on Sundays, rather than banning them outright. Critics of that idea say time limits are difficult to enforce, since bylaw officers can't be everywhere at once. Council has asked staff to look at what other municipalities have done and report back in the new year. In the meantime, the town is offering a fifty-dollar rebate to residents who trade in a gas blower for an electric one. Whatever council decides, one thing seems certain: this debate will be loud.
Next, please. Hi there, how can I help you?
Hi. I was supposed to be on the two-fifteen flight to Halifax, but the board says it's cancelled. I didn't get any message from the airline at all.

I'm sorry about that. The aircraft for that flight had a mechanical problem in Toronto, so it never left. Notifications went out about twenty minutes ago, so you may just not have seen yours yet. Can I see your boarding pass?
Here you go. The thing is, I'm going to my sister's wedding. The rehearsal dinner is tomorrow at six, and the ceremony is on Saturday morning. I really can't miss it.
Okay, let me see what I can do. You were connecting through Toronto, right?
No, it was a direct flight. That's why I booked it, so I wouldn't have to worry about connections.

Right. So I have two options for you. There's a flight tonight at eleven-forty that goes through Montreal. You'd land in Halifax at about ten tomorrow morning, but the connection in Montreal is only fifty minutes, and that flight has been running late all week.
And the other option?
There's a direct flight tomorrow at seven a.m. It lands at a quarter past two in the afternoon, local time. You'd have to spend tonight in Calgary, but there's no connection to worry about.
Hmm. The overnight one gets me there earlier, but if I miss that connection, I could be stuck in Montreal all day. The morning flight still gets me in well before six.
That's how I'd look at it, too. Shall I put you on the seven o'clock?
Yes, let's do that.
So where do I stay tonight? I don't know anyone in Calgary.

Because the cancellation was caused by a mechanical problem, which is within the airline's control, you're entitled to a hotel room and meals. I'll give you a voucher for the airport hotel, plus meal vouchers for dinner tonight and breakfast. The hotel shuttle leaves from door twelve every half hour.
What about my suitcase? I already checked it.

It'll be pulled off and tagged for the morning flight, so you don't need to do anything. If you need something from it tonight, though, you'd have to wait about two hours at baggage services. Most people just ask the hotel for a toothbrush.
Ha, I think I'll do the same. Thanks, you've been really helpful.
Kevin, did you see the hydro bill came in? It's a hundred and eighty dollars this month. That's almost double what it was in September.
Seriously? That's way more than I expected. I guess it's because it's been so cold. The baseboard heaters have been running nonstop.
That's part of it, but I also wonder about your gaming setup. You're up until two in the morning most nights.
Okay, fair, but the computer doesn't use that much. I actually looked it up. It's the heaters for sure. Remember, the landlord told us this place isn't very well insulated.
Maybe. Either way, we need a plan. What if we turned the heat down to eighteen at night and when we're both out?

I'm fine with that. I sleep better when it's cooler anyway. We could also put that plastic film over the windows. My parents did it every winter, and you can get a kit at the hardware store for about twenty bucks.
Good idea. And should we keep splitting the bill fifty-fifty? I'm only home in the evenings, and you work from home three days a week.
Hmm, that's true. How about sixty-forty, then? I'll cover the bigger share, since I'm here more.
That seems fair to me. I'll e-transfer you my part tonight, and you can pay the bill.
Deal. And I'll pick up the window kit on Saturday.
Hi, I'm hoping to sign my son up for swimming lessons. He's six, and he's never really been in a pool.

Great, you've come at a good time. Winter registration opens next Monday at seven a.m. For a beginner his age, I'd recommend our Level One class. It runs on Saturday mornings or Wednesday afternoons, for eight weeks.
Saturdays would be easier for us. Do the classes fill up fast?

The Saturday ones do, usually within the first hour. You can register online, by phone or here at the front desk, but online is quickest. I'd suggest creating your family account this week, so you're ready to go the moment registration opens.
Okay. And how much is it?

Level One is ninety-six dollars for the eight weeks. But I should mention that the city has a fee assistance program. If your household income is under a certain amount, you can get up to eighty percent off most programs, including swimming.
Oh, really? How do I apply for that?

You fill out a short form and bring in a copy of your most recent tax assessment. Approval takes about two weeks, so you'd want to apply today if you'd like it in place for registration. Once you're approved, it's good for a full year.
That's really helpful. Does he need anything special for the class?
Just a swimsuit and a towel. Goggles are optional. Oh, and for children under seven, a parent needs to stay on the pool deck or in the viewing area during the lesson.
No problem. I'll take one of those forms now, then.

Good morning. An early-season snowstorm swept through the region overnight, dropping more than thirty centimetres of snow in some areas and catching many residents off guard. Forecasters had warned of heavy snow, but the storm arrived about six hours earlier than expected, while many people were still on the roads last night. Police say they responded to more than ninety collisions between eight p.m. and midnight. Most were minor, but one section of Highway 7 was closed for several hours after a transport truck slid into a ditch. That stretch has since reopened, though drivers are being asked to slow down and leave extra space. The heavy, wet snow also brought down tree branches, many of which still had their leaves. At the peak, about fourteen thousand homes were without power. The local utility says crews have restored service to all but around two thousand customers, mostly in rural areas, and they hope to have everyone reconnected by this evening. All public and Catholic schools in the district are closed today, and school buses are cancelled. The local college has moved its classes online for the day. City snowplows have been working through the night, starting with main roads and bus routes, so residential streets may not be cleared until tomorrow. Meanwhile, the city is reminding residents that the winter parking ban is now in effect, a week earlier than usual. Vehicles left on the street overnight could be ticketed or towed so that plows can get through. And the good news: temperatures are expected to climb to plus eight by the weekend, so much of this snow should be gone before long.
Thanks for staying after the meeting, you two. So, management has agreed to match whatever we raise for the food bank this December, up to five thousand dollars. I'd love for us to hit that limit.
That's great news. Last year we raised, what, twenty-two hundred? We'll need to do a lot better.
Last year the problem was that it was all one bake sale. People bought a muffin, gave two dollars, and that was it. We need something people can get excited about.
What did you have in mind?

A silent auction. I've already talked to a few businesses near the office. The bike shop said they'd donate a tune-up, and the Thai place downstairs offered a dinner for four. If we get twenty or so items, that could bring in a lot more than muffins.

I like it, but auctions take a lot of organizing. Who's tracking the bids, collecting the payments, making sure people actually pick up their prizes? We're all swamped in December with year-end reports.
There are free online auction tools now. People bid from their phones and pay by card. It pretty much runs itself.
Okay, that's less scary. Then I'd still suggest we keep the bake sale. It's small, but it's a tradition, and it gets people talking about the fundraiser.
Agreed. And about the food bank itself, they told me that what they really need right now isn't cans, it's money, because they can buy food in bulk much more cheaply than we can.
So we skip the food drive this year?
Not entirely. But maybe we focus on the things they asked for specifically, like baby formula and toiletries, instead of random canned goods.
That makes sense. I can design a poster with a short list of what they need, so people don't just bring whatever's at the back of their cupboard.
Perfect. So Bridget, you'll take the auction, Arjun, the posters and the bake sale, and I'll talk to management about how the matching will work.
Sounds like a plan.

Across the country, employers are calling workers back to the office, and the reactions have been anything but uniform. Today I want to look at three perspectives, because I think this debate is often presented as a simple fight between bosses and employees, and that's not quite accurate. Let's start with employers who want people back full-time. Their main argument isn't about keeping an eye on staff, at least not officially. It's about learning and workplace culture. A manager at a mid-sized engineering firm put it to me this way: junior staff learn by overhearing how senior people solve problems, and you can't overhear anything on a video call. She says her newest hires took twice as long to become independent when everyone worked remotely. On the other side are employees who have built their lives around working from home. For many, the biggest issue is the commute. A worker who lives an hour outside the city told me that going back five days a week would cost him ten hours a week, plus parking. He says he's just as productive at home, and his performance reviews back that up. He's not against the office. He's against driving in just to sit on video calls with colleagues in other cities. And then there's a third group that I think gets overlooked: people who actually want to go back. Younger workers sharing small apartments with roommates, for example, often have no proper place to work. Several told me they felt isolated and missed the social side of their jobs. For them, a mandate isn't a burden. It's a relief. So where does that leave us? My own view is that blanket rules, whether everyone in or everyone out, tend to fail because they ignore these differences. The organizations that seem to be doing best are the ones that set office days team by team, based on when people genuinely need to work together. That's harder to manage, of course. But it treats employees like adults, and it gives the office a purpose beyond attendance.
Hi Doug, it's Amira from unit 412. Sorry to bother you so early, but there's no hot water in my apartment. I let the tap run for almost ten minutes this morning and it stayed ice cold.
Morning, Amira. Don't worry about it. You're actually the third person on your floor to call me since six. Is it both the kitchen and the bathroom?
Both. And I ran the dishwasher late last night, so I wondered if I'd somehow used it all up.

No, a dishwasher wouldn't do that. Every unit on your side of the building shares one big tank in the basement. If three of you on the fourth floor have nothing, it's almost certainly the tank, not anything you did.
Oh, that's a relief. I was worried I'd broken something and would have to pay for it.
Okay, I've just been down to the basement. The tank itself is fine, but the igniter that lights the gas burner has burnt out. It's a small part, but it only fits that particular model.
Can you get a new one today?

The supplier has one, but they only deliver on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Today's Wednesday, so realistically you'll have hot water again by tomorrow evening. I could drive out and pick it up myself, but the property manager has to approve that, and she doesn't start until ten.
So if she says yes, it could be fixed tonight?
Maybe, but I wouldn't count on it. Even with the part in my hand, a licensed gas technician has to install it and check the burner, and ours is booked solid this afternoon.
Okay. The thing is, I have a job interview tomorrow at nine, and I really need a shower before that.

Understood. Here's what I can do. The fitness room on the ground floor has two showers, and they run off a separate small heater, so they're working fine. I'll unlock the door at six tomorrow morning. Bring your own towel, though. We stopped supplying them during the renovations.
That works. Is there anything else I should know?

Two things. Keep your hot water taps closed until I give the all-clear, because open taps can let air into the pipes while the system refills. And the manager usually gives a small rent credit when an outage lasts more than a day, but only if you report it in writing through the tenant portal. A phone call to me doesn't count.
Morning, Hannah! First real snowfall for you, eh? How are you finding it?
Honestly, it looks beautiful from the window, but I just spent forty minutes on the driveway with a shovel that's far too small. My back is already complaining.
I remember that feeling. Listen, I've got a snowblower in the garage, and I only use it for my place and Mrs. Ferreira's walk next door. You're welcome to borrow it.
That's really kind, but I wouldn't have a clue how to start it. We don't exactly get snow in Brisbane.
It's easier than a lawnmower. Tell you what, come over Saturday morning and I'll walk you through it. Ten minutes, tops.
Saturday's perfect. But I'd feel bad just taking it. Can I at least pay for the fuel?

If you insist. Fill up a gas can next time you're at the station and we'll call it even. Oh, and one more thing. The town expects you to clear the sidewalk in front of your house within a day after the snow stops. They send a warning first, and after that, a fine.
Really? Nobody told me that. I only did the driveway.
Most newcomers don't know. Do the sidewalk this afternoon and you'll be fine. And while we're at it, have you put winter tires on your car yet?
The dealer mentioned them, but I thought all-season tires would be good enough.
With the hill at the end of our street, I really wouldn't risk it. Some insurance companies even give you a small discount for having them, so they partly pay for themselves.
Okay, you've convinced me. I'll call the garage and book an appointment this week. Thanks, Gord. I owe you a coffee at the very least.
Hi, I'm calling about swimming lessons for my two kids. We just moved to the area, and I have no idea how registration works here.

Welcome to the neighbourhood! I can walk you through it. Winter registration opens online next Monday at seven in the morning. For the first week, only city residents can sign up, and then it opens to everyone. Since you live here now, you'll get that first week.
Seven in the morning. Do the classes fill up quickly?

The Saturday morning ones are usually gone within an hour. My advice is to create a family account on our website before Monday. Each account has to be checked by staff, and that can take two or three business days. If you wait until Monday morning, you won't be able to register in time.
Good to know. How do I know which level they should be in? My daughter is eight and swims quite well, but my son is five and has only splashed around in a pool.

For your son, the beginner level for his age is the obvious choice. Your daughter is harder to place. This Saturday from ten to noon, our instructors are running free assessments. She'll swim for about fifteen minutes, and they'll give you a card with her recommended level. That way you don't waste a session in a class that's too easy or too hard.
That sounds great. And if a class is full?

You can add your child to the waitlist. If a spot opens, the system emails you, and you have twenty-four hours to accept it before it goes to the next person. So keep an eye on your inbox, including the junk folder.
One more question. The fees add up with two kids. Is there any help available?

Yes, the city has a fee assistance program that covers most of the cost for eligible families. You need to apply with proof of income, like last year's tax assessment, and approval takes about two weeks. So I'd apply today if you can. It's valid for a whole year once it's approved.
Perfect. I'll set up the account tonight and bring my daughter in on Saturday.

Residents of Port Alder can now borrow a lot more than books from their public library. This week, the main branch on Harbour Street opened what it calls a Library of Things, a collection of about one hundred and forty everyday items that people need only once in a while. The shelves include drills, ladders, sewing machines, camping stoves, a pressure washer and even several pairs of snowshoes. Head librarian Carol Boateng says the idea came directly from the public. When the library asked residents last year what new services they wanted, borrowing tools and equipment was the most common request, ahead of longer opening hours. Items can be borrowed for three weeks, just like a book, and there is no extra charge. All you need is a valid library card. However, power tools are only available to borrowers over eighteen, and first-time users must watch a short safety video at the desk. The collection was paid for mostly by a local hardware store, which donated the tools, and by a small provincial grant for shelving and staff training. On opening day, there was a line out the door before nine a.m. By closing time, more than half of the items had been checked out, and staff had started a waiting list for the most popular ones, the carpet cleaner and the tile saw. The library plans to add kayaking gear and children's sports equipment next spring. It is also looking for volunteers with repair skills to help run a monthly fix-it evening, where residents can bring in broken lamps, small appliances and bicycles. Anyone interested can sign up at the information desk. For Port Alder News, I'm Dana Leblanc.
Okay, let's settle the volunteer day. Last year the beach cleanup was a disaster with the rain, so I'd like something more reliable this time. Tom, you had an idea?

I did. A home-building charity in the city takes corporate groups on Fridays. You spend the day framing walls or painting, and you can actually see what you've built by the end. People still talk about the year we did it at my old firm.

It sounds fun, but I looked into it. They need everyone on site to wear steel-toed boots and to climb ladders, and Rajiv uses a wheelchair. I don't want to plan a day where one of our team spends it sitting in the van.
Fair point. I hadn't thought about that. Could he do something else on site, like the registration desk?

He could, but that's exactly the problem. Everyone else would be together on the build, and he'd be off on his own. The food bank warehouse, on the other hand, is all on one floor. People sort donations at long tables, and anybody can do it.
I like that. But timing matters too. If we wait until after tax season, it'll be May, and the food bank told me their shelves are fullest after the holiday drives and emptiest in late spring.
So late spring is actually when they need help most. That works in our favour, then.
Exactly. And we could collect food in the office for a month beforehand, so we bring something with us instead of just turning up.
Good. I'll offer to match whatever the team collects with a cash donation from the firm. Tom, I don't want to drop the building idea completely, though.
Honestly, I'm fine with that. Maybe a few of us could do a build on our own time in the summer, and anyone who wants to can join.
That's a nice compromise. Grace, can you call the food bank and book a Friday in late May?
Will do. I'll also ask whether they have parking near the entrance, just to be sure.

City council will vote next month on whether to ban gas-powered leaf blowers within city limits, and the proposal has divided residents more sharply than anyone at city hall expected. Supporters of the ban make two main arguments. The first is noise. Many people now work from home, and they say the high-pitched whine of a gas blower next door makes phone calls and concentration almost impossible. A city survey last year found that noise from yard equipment was the most common complaint in residential areas, ahead of traffic. The second argument is pollution. Small gas engines are much less efficient than car engines, so supporters argue that an hour of leaf blowing produces a surprising amount of exhaust, and the workers holding the machines breathe it in at close range. Opponents, however, say the ban would hit small landscaping businesses hardest. One owner told council that replacing her company's equipment with battery-powered models would cost tens of thousands of dollars, and that each machine would need several spare batteries to last a full working day. Others point out that batteries lose power quickly in the cold, which matters in a city where crews are still clearing leaves in November. Between these two positions, some councillors are looking for a middle ground. One option is a gradual phase-in, with the ban starting in three years to give businesses time to replace equipment as it wears out. Another is a rebate program to cover part of the cost of switching. A third idea is a seasonal rule, allowing gas blowers only during the busy spring and fall cleanups. The councillor who introduced the proposal says she is open to changes, but she insists that doing nothing is no longer an option. Residents can submit comments online until the end of the month.
Hello, my name is Farah Haddad. I'm calling to confirm my booking for this Saturday. I just want to check what time the crew is arriving.
Sure, Ms. Haddad, let me pull that up. Okay, I have you down for a two-bedroom move, with a crew of three and a large truck, on Sunday the twenty-fourth at eight a.m.
Sunday? No, it has to be Saturday. I said Saturday when I booked, and I'm sure the email I got said Saturday too.
I'm sorry about that. It looks like the date was changed when we moved to a new booking system last week. Is Sunday not possible at all?
Not at all. My lease ends at noon on Saturday, and the new tenants are moving in that afternoon. I have to be out by then.
Okay. Let me see what I have. Our Saturday morning crews are all fully booked, unfortunately. I could give you two movers and a smaller truck at three on Saturday afternoon.
That's three hours too late, and I doubt everything would fit in a smaller truck anyway.

Right. Then here's another idea. We have a full crew free on Friday evening. They could load everything at six, keep the truck overnight in our locked yard, and deliver to your new place first thing Saturday morning.
That could actually work. I don't get the keys to my new apartment until Saturday anyway. But isn't there a charge for keeping things overnight?
Normally there's a ninety-dollar storage fee, but since this was our mistake, I'll waive it completely.
Great. Is there anything else I need to sort out for the new arrangement?

Two things. First, you'll need to reserve the elevator at both buildings, Friday evening at the old one and Saturday morning at the new one, and then send us the times. Second, a lot of newer buildings ask movers for an insurance certificate before they'll let us in. I'll email ours to you today so you can pass it to the new building's manager.
Okay. And after what happened, could you send me the new booking in writing as well?
Absolutely. You'll get a confirmation email within the hour, and your deposit stays exactly the same.
Hey, Amelie. Have you seen the news? There's a smoke advisory for the whole region this weekend because of the fires up north.
I just saw it. I was hoping it would clear by Friday, but the forecast says it'll get worse, not better. I guess the camping trip is off.
I think so. Two nights in a tent breathing that air isn't my idea of fun. And with your asthma, it's really not worth the risk.
Yeah, my doctor told me to stay indoors as much as possible when the air quality is this bad. What about the campsite fee? We paid sixty dollars for it.

I checked the park website. Normally you lose the money if you cancel less than three days before, but because of the advisory, they're giving full refunds this week. You just have to cancel online before Friday at midnight.
Oh, good. I booked it on my account, so I'll do it tonight and send you your half.
No rush. So what should we do instead? I'd hate to just sit at home all weekend.
Well, the science centre downtown has a new exhibit about space. And it's indoors with good ventilation, which is exactly what I need right now.
I've been wanting to see that. Saturday, then? We could grab lunch at that ramen place across the street afterwards.
Sounds perfect. And let's rebook the campsite for the long weekend in September. Hopefully the fire season will be over by then.
Good idea. Those spots go fast, though, so book it when you cancel this one.
Thanks for meeting me, Joanne. My wife and I received our health cards last week, but we still don't have a family doctor, and everyone tells me it's very difficult to find one.

It can take time, so the most important thing is to get on the list right away. The province has an online registry for people who need a family doctor. You fill in one form for the whole household, and when a doctor near you is accepting patients, they contact you.
How long does that usually take?

Honestly, it varies a lot, from a few weeks to more than a year. People with young children or ongoing health conditions are often matched sooner, so be sure to mention your daughter's age and anything relevant on the form. Don't leave those boxes blank.
And in the meantime, if one of us gets sick?

You have a few options. There are walk-in clinics, and some of them let you check the wait time online and reserve a place in line, which saves you sitting in a waiting room for hours. Many clinics also offer virtual appointments by phone or video. And for some minor problems, like a simple skin rash or a prescription refill, pharmacists here can now assess you and even prescribe certain medications.
I didn't know pharmacists could do that. What about the emergency department?

That's for serious or urgent problems, like chest pain or a bad injury. If you're not sure how serious something is, you can call the provincial health line any time, day or night, and speak to a nurse who will tell you where to go.
That's very helpful. Is there anything I should bring when we finally get a doctor?

Yes, gather your medical records from home, especially your daughter's vaccination record. Schools here ask for proof of vaccinations, so having it translated now will save you a headache in September. I can give you a list of certified translators before you leave.

Commuters in Westbrook will soon have a faster way to get between the university and downtown. The city's transit agency announced today that a new express bus route will begin service on the first Monday of next month. The route, which will be numbered 90, will run every ten minutes during the morning and afternoon rush hours and every twenty minutes the rest of the day. Unlike the current Route 12, which stops about every two blocks, the express will make only eight stops, mostly at major intersections and at the central transit station. The agency says this should cut the trip from about forty minutes to around twenty-five. Fares will not change, and transfers between the express and regular buses will be free within ninety minutes. To pay for the new service, the agency will reduce Route 12 to every fifteen minutes and remove four of its least-used stops. Transit planner Ingrid Solberg says passenger counts show that fewer than ten people a day board at each of those stops, and that all of them are within a short walk of another stop. Not everyone is pleased, however. A group of seniors who live near one of the stops being removed say even a short extra walk is difficult in winter, when sidewalks are icy. The agency says it is listening. It will hold two public information sessions next week, one at the downtown library and one online, and it has promised to review the stop changes after six months. The new buses will also be the agency's first fully electric vehicles. They will charge overnight at the main garage, and the agency hopes to convert more routes over the next five years. For Westbrook Today, I'm Marcus Bell.

Next item. We've had six requests this year from owners who want to charge electric cars in the parking garage. I think we need a policy before people start running extension cords from their storage lockers.

I agree we need a policy. My suggestion is that we install chargers for everyone, maybe twenty to start, and pay for them out of the reserve fund. More buyers are asking about chargers, so it would raise the value of every unit.

I have to disagree there, Sanjay. The reserve fund is for repairs to the building, like the roof and the elevators. Our last study said the roof needs replacing within five years. If we spend that money on chargers, we'll end up with a special assessment, and owners who don't even drive will be paying for other people's cars.
But eventually most people will drive electric. We'd just be getting ahead of it.
Maybe eventually. Right now, it's six owners out of a hundred and twenty.

Before we argue about who pays, there's a more basic question. Nobody knows if the building's electrical system can even handle twenty chargers. When my sister's building looked into it, the answer was no, not without an expensive upgrade.
That's a fair point. So we'd need an electrical engineer to assess it first.
Right. And I'd suggest a user-pay model. Owners who want a charger pay for their own unit and installation, and the electricity is metered so each person pays for what they use.
I can live with that, as long as the study plans for future demand, not just the six people asking today. Otherwise, we'll have to do this all over again in three years.
No objection to that. A study doesn't commit us to anything.

Good. Then I'll get three quotes for the electrical study. Sanjay, could you put together a short survey asking owners whether they're likely to buy an electric car in the next five years? That will give the engineer something to work with.
Happy to. I'll have a draft for the next meeting.

For years, the town of Cedar Falls has not allowed residents to keep chickens in their backyards. Now a group of residents is asking council to change that rule, and the debate has been lively. Those in favour say a few hens can provide a family with fresh eggs almost every day, which is attractive at a time when grocery prices keep rising. Parents in the group also see an educational benefit. One mother told council that caring for hens has taught her children more about where food comes from than any school project. Supporters add that chickens eat kitchen scraps and produce manure that can be composted, so less waste ends up in the garbage. Opponents, however, have raised several concerns. The most common is noise, especially from roosters, which can crow before sunrise. Others worry about smell and about chicken feed attracting rats, raccoons and even coyotes into residential neighbourhoods. A local veterinarian also reminded council that birds can carry diseases, including avian flu, and that owners need to know how to keep their flocks healthy and report sick birds. Interestingly, some opponents say they are not against chickens as such. Their real concern is enforcement. They doubt the town has enough staff to inspect coops or respond to complaints. In response, council is considering a two-year pilot project. Up to fifty households would receive a permit to keep a maximum of four hens. Roosters would be banned completely, coops would have to be at least three metres from the property line, and permit holders would need to complete a short online course on bird care and disease prevention. At the end of the pilot, council would review complaints before deciding whether to make the rule permanent. A final vote is expected in the spring.

Good morning, and here is a quick reminder for everyone who uses the city bus and light rail system. Starting on the first of next month, single paper tickets will no longer be sold on buses. Instead, riders will need to tap a fare card or a bank card when they board. The good news is that the price of a single trip is staying the same, and anyone who takes more than two trips in one day will not pay for a third. Fare cards can be picked up for free at libraries, community centres and most pharmacies, and you can add money to them online or at any station machine. Seniors and students who already have a discount pass do not need to do anything, because their passes will keep working as normal. If you have questions, the customer service line is open seven days a week.

Welcome back to the show. Today I want to talk about something that sounds boring but can honestly change your month: tracking where your money goes. Most people know roughly what they pay for rent and bills, but the small daily purchases are a mystery. A coffee here, a delivery fee there, a subscription you forgot about. On their own they look tiny, but together they can add up to hundreds of dollars. So here is my challenge. For just two weeks, write down every single thing you spend money on, no matter how small. Don't try to change your habits yet, just record them. At the end, put everything into groups and look at the totals. Most listeners who have tried this tell me they were surprised, and many found at least one cost they could cut without missing it at all. The point isn't to feel guilty. It's simply to make decisions with real information.

Right, thanks everyone for joining this quick briefing. As you know, most of us now work from home two or three days a week, and on busy days the office has been running out of desks. So from Monday we are moving to a booking system. You will reserve a desk through the staff app up to one week ahead, and you can book a whole day or just a morning or afternoon. If your plans change, please cancel by nine o'clock on the day, so someone else can use the space. Teams that need to sit together for planning sessions can book one of the group areas on the second floor. We know some people prefer a regular spot, and that is understandable, but personal items will need to be cleared from desks each evening and stored in the lockers. We will review how it is going after a month, so please send any feedback to the facilities team.

People often ask me how our community garden got started, and the honest answer is that it began with a complaint. There was an empty lot at the end of our street that was full of weeds and rubbish, and a few neighbours were annoyed about it. Instead of just complaining, we asked the local council whether we could use the land. It took a few months of meetings, but they agreed to lend it to us as long as we kept it tidy. Now we have twenty-four small plots, and families grow vegetables, herbs and flowers. What surprised me most is not the food, though. It's the way people talk to each other now. Neighbours who lived next door for years without saying hello now share tools, swap seedlings and help each other out. If you're thinking of doing something similar, my advice is to start small and get the council involved early.

Hello everyone, and welcome. I work at the main branch of the public library, and I'm here tonight because many newcomers don't realise how much the library offers beyond books. First, a library card is free for anyone who lives in the city, and you only need one piece of identification and proof of your address. With that card, you can borrow books, films and even laptops for up to two weeks. We also run free conversation circles every Tuesday and Thursday evening, where you can practise English in a relaxed group. Many people tell me these circles helped them make their first friends here. If you're looking for work, our staff can help you write a resume or search for jobs online, and you can book a private room for a video interview. Finally, there are story times for young children on weekend mornings. Please take a brochure on your way out.

So a lot of you have written in asking whether using your phone in bed is really that bad for sleep. The short answer is that it depends on how you use it. The light from a screen can make your brain feel a bit more alert, but for most people the bigger problem is what they're doing on the phone. Scrolling through news or social media keeps your mind busy and often makes you feel anxious or excited, which is the opposite of what you need before sleep. It's also very easy to lose track of time, so one more video turns into an extra hour awake. My suggestion is not to ban your phone completely, because that rarely lasts. Instead, try putting it on the other side of the room thirty minutes before bed, and replace it with something calmer, like reading a paper book or listening to quiet music.

Okay team, before we start the shift, a few words about winter safety. Last year most of our injuries between December and March were not caused by machines or heavy lifting. They were slips and falls, usually near the loading doors, where snow gets carried in on boots and turns into water on the concrete. So we're making some changes. There will be extra mats at every door, and the cleaning crew will check those areas every hour instead of twice a shift. But equipment alone won't solve this. If you see a wet patch, don't walk around it and leave it for the next person. Put out one of the yellow warning signs and report it on the radio. Also, please make sure you're wearing the winter boots with proper grip. If yours are worn out, see me after this meeting and we'll replace them at no cost. Let's get through this season without anyone getting hurt.

This is a public health message. A heat warning is in effect for the region from tomorrow until at least Sunday, with daytime temperatures expected to stay above thirty-five degrees and very warm nights. Heat can be dangerous for anyone, but the people most at risk are older adults, young children, people with long-term health conditions and those who work outdoors. Please drink water regularly, even before you feel thirsty, and avoid strenuous activity in the middle of the day. If your home becomes very hot, spend a few hours somewhere cool, such as a shopping centre or one of the public cooling centres, which will open extended hours this week. Never leave children or pets in a parked car, even for a few minutes. Finally, take a moment to check on elderly neighbours or relatives who live alone, because they may not notice the warning signs of heat illness themselves.

When we decided to buy our flour and dairy from farms within about a hundred kilometres, plenty of people told me it was a lovely idea that would ruin the business. And to be fair, our costs did go up, by roughly twelve percent in the first year. What I hadn't expected was how much the change would affect everything else. Deliveries became more reliable, because when there was a problem I could phone the farmer directly instead of waiting on a large distributor. The quality of the bread improved, and customers noticed. We started printing the names of our suppliers on the menu board, and that became something people talked about. So although our prices are slightly higher than the supermarket's, our sales have grown steadily. I wouldn't say local sourcing is right for every business. It works for us because our customers value knowing where their food comes from, and they're willing to pay a little more for that.

Thanks for coming out tonight. Many of you have asked about the home energy program, so let me explain how it works. The idea is to help homeowners reduce heating costs, which, as you know, are a big expense in our winters. The first step is a home energy assessment. An advisor visits, checks where heat is escaping, and gives you a report with recommended upgrades, such as adding insulation in the attic, sealing gaps around windows or replacing an old furnace. Here's the important part: you must complete the assessment before you start any work, otherwise you won't qualify for a rebate. Once the upgrades are done, the advisor comes back for a second visit to confirm the improvements, and the rebate is paid a few weeks later. The amount depends on which upgrades you choose. In many homes, simple changes like insulation and draught sealing give the biggest savings for the lowest cost.

If you're about to rent your first apartment, here are a few things I wish someone had told me. Before you sign anything, visit the place in person, ideally in the evening, so you can hear how noisy the building is. Take photos of every room on the day you move in, especially any marks on the walls or floors. That way, if there's a disagreement about damage when you leave, you have proof. Read the lease carefully and ask the landlord to explain anything unclear, like who pays for heating or whether you can have a pet. And please, never send a deposit to someone you haven't met for a place you haven't seen. That's one of the most common rental scams. Finally, get tenant insurance. It's usually cheaper than people expect, and it protects your belongings if there's a fire or a break-in.

Registration for fall programs at the Riverside Community Centre opens this Saturday at nine a.m. This season we're adding two new options: a beginner pickleball class for adults on Monday evenings and a cooking club for teenagers on Wednesdays after school. Our popular swimming lessons for children are back, but please note that spaces fill up within hours, so we recommend registering online rather than waiting in line at the front desk. Seniors can once again join the morning walking group, which is free and meets at the main entrance every weekday at eight. For families on a lower income, a fee assistance program can reduce the cost of most programs by up to half. Application forms are available at the front desk or on our website.

I'd like to take five minutes to go over the new expense process, which starts next month. At the moment, you fill in a paper form, attach your receipts and leave it in the finance tray, and it can take up to six weeks to be paid. From now on, everything goes through the expenses app. You simply take a photo of each receipt, choose a category, and submit it. Your manager will get a notification and should approve it within five working days. Once it's approved, the money will be paid into your account with your next salary. Two important rules haven't changed: claims must be submitted within sixty days of the purchase, and alcohol still can't be claimed. Please keep your original receipts for three months, in case finance needs to check anything. If you have trouble with the app, the help desk is running short training sessions next week.

You asked what's changed at our clinic this year. Well, the biggest change is that patients can now save their place in line online before they arrive. Before, people would come at seven in the morning and wait outside, sometimes in the cold, just to be seen. Now they can check the estimated waiting time on their phone and come in when it's nearly their turn. We've also added a nurse who handles minor problems, like prescription renewals or small cuts, so doctors can spend more time on complex cases. Not everything is perfect, of course. Some older patients find the online system confusing, so we still keep a few spaces each day for people who simply walk in. And on Mondays, we're still very busy, because many people wait over the weekend. My advice is to come mid-week if your problem isn't urgent.

Thank you all for your interest in volunteering with us. I want to be honest about what the work involves, so there are no surprises. Most shifts are three hours long, and you'll spend much of that time on your feet, sorting donations, checking dates on food packages and packing boxes. You don't need any experience, and we'll train you on your first day. What we do ask is that you commit to at least one shift a month for six months, because training new people takes time. Some volunteers worry about meeting the families who use the food bank. In our experience, the most important thing is simply to be friendly and respectful. Many of the people we help are working, but their wages just don't cover rising rents and grocery prices. Last year, our volunteers gave more than eight thousand hours, and honestly, we couldn't run without them.

On today's episode, we're talking about buying a used car without getting burned. My first tip is to decide on your total budget before you start looking, and remember to include insurance, registration and repairs, not just the price of the car. Second, always get a vehicle history report. It can tell you whether the car has been in a serious accident or whether the mileage looks suspicious. Third, and this is the one people skip, pay a mechanic you trust to inspect the car before you buy it. It might cost you around a hundred dollars, but it can save you thousands. Some sellers will say the car has just been checked, and that may be true, but you want someone who's working for you, not for them. Finally, take a proper test drive that includes highway speeds, not just a few minutes around the block.

When I opened the coworking space, I assumed my members would be young freelancers and start-up founders. That turned out to be only half the story. A growing number are employees of large companies who are allowed to work remotely but find that working from the kitchen table every day is lonely and distracting. Their employers sometimes pay the membership, because it's still cheaper than renting an office. What people value most surprised me as well. I thought it would be the fast internet and the free coffee, and those matter, but members say the main reason they stay is the sense of routine and the people around them. That said, the business isn't easy. Demand drops sharply in the summer and over the holidays, so I've had to offer flexible monthly plans rather than long contracts. And competition is increasing, because cafes and even hotels now rent out workspace by the hour.

Thank you for coming to this information session. As you know, the school board is considering moving the start time at our two high schools from eight to eight forty-five. The main reason is sleep. Teenagers' body clocks naturally shift later during adolescence, so many students simply can't fall asleep early, and they arrive at school tired. Schools in other districts that have made similar changes generally report better attendance in first period. However, I don't want to pretend there are no costs. A later start means a later finish, which affects after-school jobs and sports practices. It also means rearranging bus routes, because the same buses currently serve both the elementary and high schools. Some parents have told us they rely on older children to look after younger siblings after school, and a later finish could make that difficult. No decision has been made yet, and we want to hear your views before the vote in March.

Drivers, please plan ahead this Sunday. Because of the city marathon, Lakeshore Drive will be closed in both directions from six in the morning until two in the afternoon. Several downtown streets will also close for shorter periods as runners pass through. Bus routes along the waterfront will be diverted, and extra trains will run on the subway line all morning. If you need to get downtown, the easiest option is to leave your car at home and take the train.

Just a quick note before lunch. We'll be holding a fire drill this Thursday at around ten thirty. When the alarm sounds, please stop what you're doing, leave your bags and laptops behind, and use the nearest stairwell, not the lifts. Our meeting point is the car park across the road, next to the blue sign. Floor wardens will be wearing orange vests, and they'll check that everyone is out. Please don't go back inside until a warden tells you it's safe.

I used to think meal planning was only for very organised people, and I'm definitely not one of them. What changed my mind was realising how much food I was throwing away.
