Let's look at how many bats find their way in complete darkness. The technique is called echolocation. A bat produces a series of very high-pitched calls, mostly far above the range of human hearing, and then listens for the echoes that bounce back from objects around it. The time it takes for an echo to return tells the bat how far away something is, and subtle differences between what each ear hears tell it the direction. What's remarkable is how the bat adjusts its calls. While it's simply cruising, it calls slowly, perhaps ten times a second. But as it closes in on an insect, the calls speed up dramatically, into what researchers call a feeding buzz, sometimes well over a hundred calls a second. That gives the bat rapid updates on exactly where its prey is moving. And it's worth adding that some moths have evolved ways to fight back, for example by hearing the calls and diving out of the way.

One of the most useful ideas in economics is opportunity cost. Put simply, the opportunity cost of any choice is the value of the best alternative you give up. Because our time, money and resources are limited, choosing one thing always means not choosing something else. Let me give you an everyday example. Say you spend a Saturday afternoon at a concert. The ticket price is obvious, but the real cost also includes whatever else you could have done with those hours, maybe a paid shift at work or time studying for an exam. Economists argue that people often ignore these hidden costs and focus only on money. The same thinking applies to governments. If a city spends its budget on a new stadium, the opportunity cost might be the schools or clinics that money could have built instead. So whenever you make a decision, it helps to ask not just what it costs, but what you are giving up.

Linguists estimate that there are around seven thousand languages spoken in the world today, yet a large proportion of them are considered endangered. A language rarely disappears suddenly. Instead, the process is usually gradual and generational. It typically begins when a community comes under economic or social pressure to use a dominant language, perhaps for schooling, employment or contact with government. Parents, wanting the best opportunities for their children, start speaking the dominant language at home. Those children may still understand their grandparents' language, but they don't use it actively, and so their own children never learn it at all. Within three generations, a language can go from thriving to having only a handful of elderly speakers. Why does this matter? Each language encodes knowledge, for instance detailed vocabulary for local plants, ecosystems and traditions, which may not be recorded anywhere else. The encouraging news is that revitalisation is possible. Immersion schools, community recordings and even mobile apps have helped some communities bring young speakers back to their ancestral languages.

Today it seems obvious that everyone in a region shares the same clock time, but this is actually quite a recent arrangement. Until the nineteenth century, most towns kept their own local time, based on the position of the sun. When the sun was highest in the sky, it was noon. This meant that a town a little further west would be several minutes behind its neighbour. For centuries nobody really minded, because travel was slow. The railways changed all that. Once trains could cover long distances in a few hours, dozens of different local times made timetables confusing and even dangerous, since two trains on the same line might be working from different clocks. So railway companies began adopting a single standard time across their networks. In Britain, railway time spread during the eighteen forties, and in North America the railways introduced standard time zones in eighteen eighty-three. The following year, an international conference chose Greenwich as the prime meridian, laying the foundation for the global system of time zones we use now.

I'd like to introduce a thinking error that affects all of us, called confirmation bias. Confirmation bias is our tendency to search for, notice and remember information that supports what we already believe, while ignoring or explaining away information that challenges it. Imagine someone who believes a particular diet works. They'll remember the friend who lost weight on it, but forget the three friends who didn't. The same thing happens online. If you search for evidence that a product is excellent, you'll usually find it, partly because of the way you phrased the question. Now, why does this matter for you as students? In research, confirmation bias can lead scientists to design studies that can only prove them right. That's why good scientific practice deliberately looks for disconfirming evidence. A practical tip: when you're writing an essay, try to state the strongest version of the opposing argument before you respond to it. It's one of the simplest ways to keep your own thinking honest.

When we talk about carbon dioxide emissions, we usually focus on the atmosphere. But a substantial share of the carbon dioxide we release, roughly a quarter, is actually absorbed by the oceans. In one sense that's helpful, because it slows down warming. The problem is chemical. When carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater, it forms carbonic acid, and this gradually lowers the pH of the ocean. Since the start of the industrial era, the average pH of surface seawater has fallen by about zero point one units. That sounds tiny, but because the pH scale is logarithmic, it represents roughly a thirty percent increase in acidity. The organisms most at risk are those that build shells or skeletons from calcium carbonate, such as corals, oysters and certain kinds of plankton. In more acidic water, the carbonate they need becomes less available, so building shells takes more energy, and in extreme cases existing shells can begin to dissolve. And because plankton sit at the base of marine food webs, the effects could spread far beyond the species directly affected.

The proposal is that all first-year students would have to live in university residence. I'm in favour. Your first year is when you build your social network, and living on campus makes that so much easier. Students who commute often tell me they feel disconnected.

I understand the social argument, but making it compulsory worries me. Residence fees are expensive, and for local students who could live at home for free, it's a huge extra cost. That could actually discourage some people from applying at all.
I think the data on retention is relevant here. Students who live on campus in first year tend to be more likely to continue into second year. So there's an academic benefit as well as a social one.

Maybe, but is that because of the residence itself, or because the students who choose residence are already better off and more confident? Forcing everyone in won't automatically produce the same result.
That's a fair challenge. Perhaps the university could offer bursaries so cost isn't a barrier, and exempt students with caring responsibilities or family commitments.

Or, instead of a requirement, they could make residence the default but let people opt out, and invest in programmes that connect commuter students with campus life. That keeps most of the benefits without the unfairness.

Our department wants to replace printed textbooks with free online textbooks. I think it's brilliant. Some of the books on my reading list cost over a hundred dollars each, and students shouldn't have to choose between food and course materials.
I agree about the cost, but I actually learn better from paper. I can annotate it, and I'm not distracted by notifications. Reading long chapters on a screen gives me headaches.
My concern is quality. Commercial textbooks go through careful editing. Are free online ones reviewed in the same way, and will they be kept up to date?
Many of them are written and reviewed by academics, and because they're digital, they can be updated much faster than a printed edition. Lecturers can also adapt them to fit the course.
If that's true, then my only request is that students can print them cheaply, or that the library keeps a few printed copies for people like me.
That sounds reasonable. I'd support it as long as each book is checked by the department before it's adopted. Then we save money without lowering standards.

The student union is asking the university to sell all its investments in fossil fuel companies. I strongly support that. A university that teaches climate science while profiting from oil and coal is sending a contradictory message.

I'm sympathetic, but I'm not convinced divestment changes anything. If the university sells its shares, someone else simply buys them. The companies don't lose any money, and the university loses its voice as a shareholder.
There's also the financial side. The endowment funds scholarships. If divesting reduced returns, it could hurt students from poorer backgrounds, which would be an ethical problem of its own.

But many investors argue fossil fuel assets are becoming riskier anyway, as regulations tighten. And the symbolic effect matters. When respected institutions divest, it shifts public opinion and makes it harder for those companies to look legitimate.
Symbolism is real, I'll grant that. But I'd rather see the university use its shareholder votes to push companies towards clean energy targets, and divest only if they refuse to change.
A staged approach like that seems wise. Set clear deadlines, protect the scholarship budget, and publish an annual report so students can see what's actually happening.

Our faculty is considering replacing final exams with continuous coursework, like weekly tasks and projects. I'm all for it. A single three-hour exam rewards people who perform well under pressure, not necessarily people who understand the subject.
I'd disagree a bit. Exams are one of the few assessments where you know the work is genuinely the student's own. With coursework, it's much harder to rule out heavy outside help or copying.

I see both sides. Coursework spreads the workload, which is better for wellbeing, but it can also mean you're constantly under deadline pressure. Some students find that more stressful than one exam period.
True, but the feedback is the key advantage. With weekly tasks you find out what you're getting wrong while there's still time to fix it. After an exam, the course is already over.
I accept that feedback matters. Maybe a mix would work, with coursework for learning and a shorter supervised exam to confirm individual understanding.
I'd support that, as long as deadlines across different courses are coordinated so students don't end up with five assignments due in the same week.

There's a proposal to make a six-month work placement compulsory in every degree. I think it's overdue. Employers keep saying graduates lack practical experience, and placements give students contacts and a clearer idea of what career they actually want.

In principle I agree, but who gets the good placements? Students with family connections or who can afford to move to a big city will get the best ones. And if placements are unpaid, poorer students simply can't take them.

I'd add that it doesn't fit every discipline equally. In engineering or nursing a placement is obviously valuable, but for a philosophy or history student, finding something relevant for six months could be really difficult.
Those are fair points, but the skills are transferable. A history student working in a museum or a policy office still learns teamwork, deadlines and professional communication.
Then the university has to guarantee that every placement is paid, and use its own careers service to allocate them fairly rather than leaving students to compete through personal networks.

And maybe allow flexibility. Departments could offer alternatives such as a research project with an external partner, or shorter placements, so students in every field get experience without a one-size-fits-all rule.

Today I want to talk about something you have probably felt without naming it: the urban heat island. On a summer evening, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. Why? Well, there are three main reasons. First, materials like concrete, asphalt and brick absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night. Second, cities have far less vegetation, so there is less shade and less cooling from moisture evaporating off leaves. And third, human activity itself, from traffic to air conditioning units, pumps extra heat into the streets. Now, this is not just a matter of comfort. During heatwaves, these extra degrees can be dangerous, particularly for elderly residents. So planners are experimenting with solutions: lighter-coloured roofs that reflect sunlight, more street trees, and small parks spread throughout neighbourhoods rather than one large park on the edge of town.

Let me ask you a question. If you have six hours to prepare for an exam, is it better to study for six hours the night before, or for one hour a day over six days? Most of you probably know the answer, but many of you still choose the first option. Psychologists call the advantage of the second approach the spacing effect. When we spread our study sessions out, we give ourselves time to partly forget the material. That sounds like a bad thing, right? But actually, the effort of recalling something we have half forgotten is exactly what strengthens the memory. Cramming, by contrast, feels productive because the information is fresh, but it tends to fade within days. So, my practical advice is this: plan short, regular review sessions, and test yourself rather than simply rereading your notes. It is less comfortable, but the results last much longer.

In this part of the lecture, I would like to look at microfinance, which means providing very small loans to people who are excluded from conventional banking. The original idea was quite simple. Many people in low-income communities have business ideas, perhaps buying a sewing machine or extra stock for a market stall, but no bank will lend to them because they have no collateral. Microfinance institutions addressed this by lending to small groups, where members share responsibility for repayment. In the early years, repayment rates were remarkably high, and microfinance was celebrated as a powerful tool against poverty. However, more recent evaluations have been more cautious. Many studies have found that while borrowers gain flexibility and can manage emergencies more easily, the average effect on household income is fairly modest. Some borrowers have also fallen into debt by taking loans from several lenders at once. So the current view is more balanced: microfinance is useful, but it is not a cure for poverty on its own.

Antibiotics are among the most important medical discoveries of the twentieth century, but their effectiveness is under threat. The problem is antibiotic resistance. Whenever we use an antibiotic, most of the target bacteria die, but a few may survive because of random genetic differences. Those survivors multiply, and over time the whole population can become resistant. Now, this is a natural evolutionary process, but human behaviour has accelerated it enormously. Antibiotics are often prescribed for viral infections, such as colds, where they do nothing at all. Patients sometimes stop a course early once they feel better. And in some countries, large quantities are given to farm animals simply to promote growth. The consequences are serious: routine operations and minor infections could become far riskier. So, what can be done? Responses include stricter prescribing, better hygiene in hospitals, reducing agricultural use, and investing in new drugs, which, frankly, is commercially unattractive for many pharmaceutical companies.

So the university is proposing to record every lecture and put it online. Personally, I think it is a great idea. If you are ill, or you work part-time, you do not fall behind, and you can rewatch the difficult parts before exams. It also makes revision much less stressful.

I see the benefits, but I am worried about attendance. If everything is online, a lot of students will just stop coming. And honestly, the live discussion and being able to ask questions are the most valuable parts of a lecture. You cannot interrupt a video to ask what something means.

I think you are both right, actually. The evidence I have seen suggests attendance does drop a little, but mostly among students who were already skipping. For students who speak English as a second language, recordings are incredibly helpful, because they can slow them down or check terminology.
That is a fair point about language. But what about lecturers? Some of them may become more cautious and avoid saying anything controversial if they know it is being recorded.
Maybe lecturers could pause the recording for discussion sections. That would protect open debate while still keeping the core content available.
Exactly, a flexible policy seems sensible. Record the main content, let staff opt out of certain segments, and keep the live sessions interactive so there is still a reason to attend in person.

The student union wants the main canteen to go completely meat-free two days a week. I am in favour. Meat production has a large carbon footprint, and the university has committed to cutting its emissions.

I agree with the goal, but I am not sure banning things is the right method. People resent being told what to eat. They might just buy burgers off campus instead, which would not reduce emissions at all, and the canteen would lose income.

There is also a cost issue. Plant-based meals can be cheaper, but the ones on offer here are often more expensive, and that hits students on tight budgets hardest. Some of my friends already skip lunch to save money.

Okay, but if the canteen redesigned the menu properly, with good lentil dishes and curries, it could easily be cheaper. The problem is the current menu, not the idea. Plenty of cuisines around the world are mainly vegetarian.
That is what I would prefer: make the vegetarian options the default and the most attractive, and leave meat available. Small nudges often change behaviour more than strict rules.
I could support that, as long as prices are fair. Perhaps run a one-semester trial, measure sales and emissions, and then let students vote on whether to go further.
A trial with real data sounds reasonable. I would still push for meat-free days eventually, but starting with defaults is better than doing nothing.

Our department needs a policy on AI writing tools. My instinct is to allow them for brainstorming and editing, but to require students to declare exactly how they were used. Something like a short statement attached to each assignment.

As a student representative, I think that is realistic. These tools are already everywhere, and employers expect graduates to use them. Banning them would just be unenforceable, because detection software is unreliable and sometimes flags work that students genuinely wrote themselves.

I understand that, but my concern is that essays are meant to develop thinking, not just produce a text. If a tool structures the argument, the student may never learn to do it themselves. Building an argument is one of the core skills we are supposed to be teaching, and a declaration does not really solve that.
Then maybe the assessment should change. More in-class writing, oral defences of essays, or submitting drafts so tutors can see how the work developed.

Oral defences are appealing, but they take a great deal of staff time with large classes. Some of our first-year modules have more than three hundred students. Draft submission is more practical, and it also discourages last-minute work.
I could accept a combination: permitted use with a declaration, drafts submitted for major essays, and at least one supervised writing task each year, so we know students can argue independently.

You are working on a group project with three classmates. Yesterday you missed an important planning meeting because your train was cancelled, and you forgot to let anyone know. Your group leader, Sam, has just sent a message asking whether you are still committed to the project. You decide to call Sam. What would you say to Sam?

You live in a student apartment building. For the past week, your neighbor has been playing loud music late at night, and you have an important exam in two days. You have never spoken to this neighbor before and want to stay on good terms. You knock on their door one evening. What would you say to your neighbor?

You have been unwell with a severe flu for the past week and have a doctor's certificate. As a result, you have not been able to finish an essay that is due this Friday. You see your tutor, Dr. Lewis, in the corridor after class and decide to ask for an extension. What would you say to Dr. Lewis?

You manage a small office and ordered fifty boxes of printer paper from a supplier for an important event next week. The delivery arrived today, but it contained only twenty boxes, and the invoice charges you for fifty. You call the supplier's customer service line to sort out the problem. What would you say to the customer service representative?
